1.  How does Alison Zicari explain the natural event that gives rise to a cenote?
   ■ A river slowly dries up over time.
   ■ A cave ceiling collapses and reveals hidden water.

   ■  Earthquakes open giant cracks in the soil.
2.  Why does the Yucatán Peninsula contain such a high concentration
     of cenotes?
   ■   It was once part of a flat desert that eroded quickly over time.
   ■   It is built of giant old volcanic rocks.
   ■   It used to be a coral formation that became exposed.
   ■   It receives more rain than any other area in Mexico.

     Peninsula are formed by
   ■  rapidly melting ice.
   ■  water travelling through rock beneath the surface.
   ■  lakes draining into deep reservoirs.
   ■  ocean waves carving inland tunnels.
4.  What have researchers gained from studying cenotes and their connected
     caves?
   ■  Maps of modern underwater cave systems.
   ■  Evidence of ancient life, both human and animal.

   ■  Proof that the Maya invented scuba diving.

   ■  They look for protection and need a quiet shelter.

SÈRIE 2


I. Listening comprehension (3 points)

                   THE WORLD OF CENOTES

In this podcast you are going to hear some new words. Read and listen to them. Make
sure you know what they mean.



limestone: pedra calcària/caliza

coral reef: escull de coral/arrecife de coral

jade: jade/jade

manatee: manatí/manatí





Ready? Now read the questions on the following page. Read them carefully before
listening to the podcast. [Now listen to the interview.]



Journalist: Ms. Zicari, thank you for joining us today. You’re known as one of the top
experts on cenotes. To begin, could you explain to our listeners what a cenote actually
is?

Alison Zicari: Thank you for having me. A cenote is a natural hole in the ground. It
forms when the roof of an underground cave collapses and allows us to see the water
inside. The word “cenote” usually describes an underground chamber filled with
permanent water.

Journalist: Where can people find these cenotes?

AZ: You can find cenotes in several parts of the world, but the best-known and largest
concentration is in Mexico, especially on the Yucatán Peninsula. This whole peninsula
is made from limestone, which used to be a huge coral reef millions of years ago.
When the sea level dropped, the reef was exposed, and over time, it became full of
caves, tunnels, and holes. Today, the land’s almost completely flat, but underneath it’s
a giant network of underground rivers filled with rainwater that travels through cracks in
the limestone filling caves which sometimes collapse creating cenotes. Scientists
estimate that there’re more than 7,000 cenotes in the Yucatán.
                                                                      Pàgina 2 de 5
                                                                       Anglès
     Proves d’accés a la Universitat 2026, convocatòria extraordinària. Criteri específic d'avaluació


Journalist: That number is incredible. Can you tell us more about the cave systems
connected to cenotes?

AZ: Yes, the Yucatán is home to some of the world’s longest underwater cave
systems. One of the most famous is Sistema Sac Actun, located in the Riviera Maya. It
stretches about 350 kilometers and reaches a depth of around 119 meters. Explorers
and archaeologists have found many important remains inside these caves, including
9,000-year-old human bones and the bones of animals that lived during the ice age.
These discoveries tell us that humans have been exploring or using these caves for
thousands of years.

Journalist: Speaking of humans, cenotes played a very important role in the Maya
civilization, didn’t they?

AZ: They certainly did. For the Maya, cenotes were not just a source of fresh water,
though that alone made them extremely valuable. They also believed cenotes were the
entrance to the underworld. According to Maya beliefs, spirits and gods visited cenotes,
especially Chaac, the god of rain, thunder, and lightning. Because of this, the Maya
built many of their temples and villages near cenotes. In fact, new research shows that
some important Maya cities—such as Chichén Itzá—were actually built directly on top
of cenotes.

Journalist: Were these cenotes used for ceremonies?

AZ: Yes. Some cenotes became sacred places for rituals and offerings. Archaeologists
have found items such as jade, gold, silver, and incense at the bottom of these
cenotes. They have also discovered human remains. At places like the Sacred Cenote
at Chichén Itzá, many of the bodies show wounds that suggest human sacrifice.
However, other cenotes contain human remains without signs of violence, so these
may have been peaceful burials, perhaps to prepare people for the next life.

Journalist: And today, people visit cenotes for very different reasons, right?

AZ: That’s right. Today cenotes are still important for water, but they’re also major
tourist attractions. Millions of visitors come every year to swim, dive, snorkel, and
explore. Some cenotes offer cultural experiences where visitors can watch modern
Maya ceremonies. These ceremonies aren’t dangerous—of course, no one’s
sacrificed—but they still include symbolic offerings like resin, cacao, seeds, corn, flower
petals, and sugar.

Journalist: There’s also a surprising connection between cenotes and the asteroid that
killed the dinosaurs. Can you explain that?

AZ: Yes, it’s a fascinating story. About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 to 15
kilometers wide crashed on the Yucatán Peninsula. The explosion released as much
energy as 100 trillion tons of TNT. This event caused huge fires, tsunamis, and climate
changes that led to the extinction of many species, including the dinosaurs. The impact
also changed the structure of the limestone underground. It made the rock weaker and
                                                                      Pàgina 3 de 5
                                                                       Anglès

easier to erode. Over millions of years, groundwater moved in special patterns around
the edge of the impact crater. This process created the “Ring of Cenotes.” The crater
itself is buried under layers of ground and ocean, so we cannot see it with our eyes, but
the ring of cenotes is still visible from space. The city of Mérida is right in the middle of
this ancient crater.

Journalist: Besides history and geology, cenotes also have interesting wildlife. Can
you tell us about that?

AZ: Yes, cenotes are important habitats for many animals. Because they’re protected
from the open ocean, they offer calm, safe spaces. Manatees, for example, sometimes
travel from the Caribbean Sea into cenotes through underwater caves. They rest there
and even nurse their young. Crocodiles also live in some cenotes. They’re part of the
natural ecosystem, and tourists need to keep a respectful distance. They’re usually
calm, but like all wild animals, they should never be disturbed.

Journalist: All of this makes cenotes sound like truly remarkable places. Any final
thoughts for our audience?

AZ: Yes. I think cenotes are some of the most unique natural wonders in the world.
They combine geology, history, culture, wildlife, and adventure in one place. They’ve
been important for thousands of years—from the time of the Maya to the present day—
and they’re still full of discoveries waiting to be made. Anyone who visits the Yucatán
should explore at least one cenote. It’s an experience you’ll never forget.

reading.examen:
Reading · PAU 2026 · Setembre · Sèrie 2

    Part 2: Reading comprehension

                     YOU MIGHT BE A LATE BLOOMER
        Today we live in a society structured to promote early bloomers. Our school system has
         sorted people by the time they are 18, using grades and university entrance exam scores.
       Some of these people zoom to prestigious academic trajectories while others get left behind.
       Many of our most prominent models of success made it big while young—Bill Gates, Mark
     5  Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Taylor Swift, Michael Jordan. Magazines publish lists to glamorize
         youthful superstars on the rise. Age discrimination is a fact of life. But for many people, the
          talents that bloom later in life are more consequential than the ones that bloom early. Even
           brilliant people apparently need at least a couple of decades to master their field.
              Successful late bloomers are all around us. Morgan Freeman had his first key roles in Street
    10  Smart and Driving Miss Daisy in his early 50s. Colonel Harland Sanders started Kentucky Fried
        Chicken in his 60s. Isak Dinesen published the book that established her literary reputation,
        Out of Africa, at 52. Morris Chang founded Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the world’s
          leading chipmaker, at 55. If Samuel Johnson had died at 40, few would remember him, but now
        he is considered one of the greatest writers in the history of the English language. Copernicus
    15  came up with his theory of planetary motion in his 60s.
         Why do some people hit their peak later than others? In his book Late Bloomers, the
          journalist Rich Karlgaard points out that late bloomers are not simply early bloomers on a
         delayed timetable—they didn’t just do the things early bloomers did but at a later age. Late
        bloomers tend to be qualitatively different. They possess a different set of abilities that are
    20  mostly invisible to or discouraged by our current education system. They usually have to invent
          their own paths. Late bloomers “fulfill their potential frequently in novel and unexpected ways,”
         Karlgaard writes, “surprising even those closest to them.”
                  If you survey history, a taxonomy of achievement emerges. In the first category are the
          “early bloomers,” the precocious geniuses. These are people like Picasso or Fitzgerald who
    25  succeeded young. As the University of Chicago economist David Galenson has pointed out,
          these high achievers usually made a conceptual breakthrough. They came up with a new
          idea and then executed it. Then there are the “second-mountain people,” exemplified by, say,
         Albert Schweitzer. First, they conquer their career mountain; Schweitzer, for instance, was an
         accomplished musician and scholar. But these people find their career success unsatisfying, so
    30  they leave their career mountain to serve humanity—their whole motivational structure shifts
        from acquisition to altruism. Schweitzer became a doctor in the poorest parts of Africa, and
       won the Nobel Peace Prize for his work in 1952. Finally, there are the people Galenson calls “the
          masters.” These are people like Cézanne or Alfred Hitchcock or Charles Darwin, who were not
             all that successful—and in some cases just not even very good at what they did—when they were
    35  young. This could have been discouraging, but they just kept improving.
              Late bloomers don’t do as much advance planning as the conceptual geniuses, but they
         regard their entire lives as experiments. They try something and learn, and then they try
        something else and learn more. Their focus is not on their finished work, which they often
        throw away haphazardly. Their focus is on the process of learning itself, which they enjoy. They
    40   live their lives as a long period of trial and error, trying this and trying that, a slow process of
         accumulation and elaboration, so the quality of their work peaks late in life. They are the ugly
         ducklings of human achievement, who, over the decades, turn themselves into swans. Slow at
         the start, late bloomers are still sprinting during that final lap—they do not slow down as age
         brings its decay. They are seeking. They are striving. They are in it with all their heart.

                                                                         Text adapted from an article by
                                                   David Brooks. The Atlantic [online] (June 26, 2024)

     breakthrough: descobriment / descubrimiento
     haphazardly: de qualsevol manera / de cualquier manera

Writing · PAU 2026 · Setembre · Sèrie 2

    Part 3: Writing

   Choose ONE topic. Your answer should be 125-150 words in length. There is no specific
    penalty for exceeding 150 words in length.
      [4 points: 1 point for grammar, 1 point for vocabulary and spelling, 1 point for cohesion, and 1 point for adequacy and
     coherence]

     1.  During your school’s Communication Week, students will take part in a debate about
        the growing impact that social media influencers have on teenagers’ behaviour, lifestyle
         choices, and opinions. You have been asked to write a for and against essay discussing
       both the positive and negative effects that influencers may have on young people. In your
          text, you should consider aspects such as the promotion of healthy or unhealthy habits,
        the reliability of sponsored content, and the pressure to conform to certain beauty or
        success standards.

     2.  Imagine working in your ideal job. Write a description of a full day at work in detail,
        beginning with how you commute to your workplace and what your morning routine is
          like. Explain your exact daily tasks and responsibilities, the people you work with, and
        the type of environment you work in. Include information about your colleagues, your
         interactions with them, and how you collaborate. Finally, explain whether you enjoy this
        job or not, giving clear reasons for your satisfaction or dissatisfaction.
